title: Theil indices
text:
Let Y be a positive random variable with mean \mu = E[Y]. The Theil indices are members of the generalised entropy family GE(\alpha):

T_1 = GE(1) = E\left[\frac{Y}{\mu}\log\frac{Y}{\mu}\right],
\qquad
T_0 = GE(0) = E\left[\log\frac{\mu}{Y}\right] = \log\mu - E[\log Y].

T_1 is the Theil index and T_0 the mean logarithmic deviation (MLD). Both are zero under perfect equality and increase with inequality. T_1 is more sensitive to the upper tail of the distribution, and T_0 to the lower tail.

title: Theil indices
text:
Additive decomposition
If the population is partitioned into G groups with population shares p_g, income shares s_g, means \mu_g and indices T_{0g}, T_{1g}:

T_1 = \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} s_g\, T_{1g}}_{\text{within}} + \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} s_g \log\frac{\mu_g}{\mu}}_{\text{between}},
\qquad
T_0 = \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} p_g\, T_{0g}}_{\text{within}} + \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} p_g \log\frac{\mu}{\mu_g}}_{\text{between}}.

This property makes the Theil indices the standard tool to identify the sources of inequality: by region, gender, age, education, sector, type of employment or municipality size.

title: Theil indices
Theil indices
text:
Jackknife bias correction and variance
Let \widehat{T}_{(i)} be the estimator computed without observation i, and \widehat{T}_{(\cdot)} = n^{-1}\sum_i \widehat{T}_{(i)}. The jackknife bias-corrected estimator and variance estimator are

\widehat{T}^{\,J} = n\,\widehat{T} - (n-1)\,\widehat{T}_{(\cdot)},
\qquad
\widehat{V}_J = \frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\widehat{T}_{(i)} - \widehat{T}_{(\cdot)}\right)^2 .

The standard implementation recomputes the index n times, with cost O(n^2). Because \widehat{T}_0 and \widehat{T}_1 depend on the data only through a few sums, every leave-one-out value can be obtained by subtracting observation i from those sums, with cost O(n):
# Leave-one-out values in O(n)
T.loo <- function(y, index = c("T1", "T0")) {
  index <- match.arg(index)
  n  <- length(y)
  Sy <- sum(y)
  m.i <- (Sy - y) / (n - 1)                      # leave-one-out means
  if (index == "T1") {
    Sylogy <- sum(y * log(y))
    (Sylogy - y * log(y)) / (Sy - y) - log(m.i)
  } else {
    Slogy <- sum(log(y))
    log(m.i) - (Slogy - log(y)) / (n - 1)
  }
}

jackknife.theil <- function(y, index = c("T1", "T0")) {
  index <- match.arg(index)
  n   <- length(y)
  est <- if (index == "T1") T1.hat(y) else T0.hat(y)
  loo <- T.loo(y, index)
  m.loo <- mean(loo)
  list(estimate  = est,
       corrected = n * est - (n - 1) * m.loo,
       variance  = (n - 1) / n * sum((loo - m.loo)^2))   # two-pass
}
These functions will be part of the R package theil, developed in WP4.

title: Research data and R code
section: Parameters for a given value of the index
text:
Parameters for a given value of the index
The following functions return the parameter of each distribution that yields a given value of T_0 or T_1, using the closed forms on the page Theil indices.
# True Theil indices
T.lognormal <- function(sigma)       sigma^2 / 2
T.pareto    <- function(alpha, index) if (index == "T1")
  1 / (alpha - 1) - log(alpha / (alpha - 1)) else log(alpha / (alpha - 1)) - 1 / alpha
T.gamma     <- function(k, index) if (index == "T1")
  digamma(k) + 1 / k - log(k) else log(k) - digamma(k)

# Parameter giving a target value of the index
param.theil <- function(T, dist = c("lognormal", "pareto", "gamma"),
                        index = c("T0", "T1")) {
  dist  <- match.arg(dist)
  index <- match.arg(index)
  switch(dist,
    lognormal = sqrt(2 * T),
    pareto    = uniroot(function(a) T.pareto(a, index) - T, c(1 + 1e-6, 1e4))$root,
    gamma     = uniroot(function(k) T.gamma(k, index)  - T, c(1e-4, 1e5))$root)
}

title: Research data and R code
section: Samples with a given Theil index
text:
Samples with a given Theil index
set.seed(123)
n <- 50
T <- 0.3

alpha <- param.theil(T, "pareto",    "T0")
sigma <- param.theil(T, "lognormal", "T0")
k     <- param.theil(T, "gamma",     "T0")

Y.Par <- rpareto(n, scale = 1, shape = alpha)
Y.Log <- rlnorm(n, meanlog = 5, sdlog = sigma)
Y.Gam <- rgamma(n, shape = k, scale = 1)

# Sample skewness: the key driver of the bias
sapply(list(Pareto = Y.Par, Lognormal = Y.Log, Gamma = Y.Gam), skewness)

title: Research data and R code
section: Monte Carlo estimate of the relative bias
text:
Monte Carlo estimate of the relative bias
RB.theil <- function(T, n, R = 1000, dist = "pareto", index = "T0") {
  p   <- param.theil(T, dist, index)
  rdist <- switch(dist,
    lognormal = function() rlnorm(n, 0, p),
    pareto    = function() rpareto(n, scale = 1, shape = p),
    gamma     = function() rgamma(n, shape = p))
  est <- replicate(R, { y <- rdist(); if (index == "T1") T1.hat(y) else T0.hat(y) })
  100 * (mean(est) - T) / T
}

RB.theil(T = 0.5, n = 50, dist = "pareto", index = "T0")
The functions T0.hat() and T1.hat() are defined on the page Theil indices.

title: THEILUMINA
text:
What this website offers
This website is a working tool for the research team and an open resource for other researchers:

Communication and collaboration. Data, R code, results and conclusions are shared among team members.
Reproducible research. Anyone can run the code and obtain the same tables and figures.
Interactivity. The bias explorer lets users see how bias changes with skewness, inequality and sample size.
Inequality observatory. The observatory shows official inequality indicators (Gini, S80/S20 and Theil indices) from Eurostat, the World Bank and the Spanish Statistical Office (INE), with links to other inequality observatories.
Dissemination and internationalisation. Results, data and software are openly available, and the project identity can be freely used by co-authors and collaborators.
Collaboration. External researchers interested in the project can contact us.

title: Research problems and questions
text: Theil indices (T_0 and T_1) are the standard tool to decompose inequality into a between-group and a within-group component. Yet the way they are usually estimated and used in practice raises several problems that the project addresses. The figures on this page are preliminary results of the team, and illustrate the problems with the most skewed distribution considered (Pareto).

title: Research problems and questions
text:
Problem 1 · The estimators underestimate inequality
The standard (plug-in) estimators of the Theil indices are biased downwards in finite samples: they systematically underestimate inequality. The bias grows with the skewness of the data and the level of inequality, which are precisely the conditions found in income, wealth, water consumption or tourism data. With highly skewed data and high inequality, samples larger than 5,000 observations are needed for the bias to become negligible.



Relative bias of the standard, jackknife bias-corrected and semiparametric estimators of T_0 (left) and T_1 (right) for samples drawn from a Pareto distribution (high skewness). The standard estimator (solid blue) shows a negative bias that reaches about −20% with small samples and high inequality; the bias-corrected estimator (dashed green) stays close to zero; the semiparametric estimator can overestimate severely (values shown as text). Source: THEILUMINA team, preliminary results.



Research questions (WP1)

RQ1. How large is the bias of the estimators of T_0 and T_1, and which data features (sample size, skewness, inequality, tails) drive it?
RQ2. Can the bias be predicted from observable sample features, so that users know in advance whether their estimate is reliable (negligible, mild, moderate or severe bias)?
RQ3. Which correction (jackknife, model-based, analytical or semiparametric) best reduces the bias without inflating the mean squared error?
RQ4. How does the bias propagate to the between- and within-group components of the decomposition?

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 2 · Inference is unreliable: variances are underestimated
text:
Problem 2 · Inference is unreliable: variances are underestimated
Even when the point estimate is acceptable, its margin of error may not be. Under skewed distributions, the usual asymptotic and bootstrap variance estimators severely underestimate the true variance (by 30–70% in the figure below), even with thousands of observations. As a result, confidence intervals are too narrow and differences in inequality across regions, groups or years may be declared significant when they are not. The jackknife variance estimator remains close to the region of negligible bias.



Relative bias of the asymptotic (solid blue), jackknife (dashed green) and bootstrap (dash-dotted red) variance estimators of the Theil indices for samples drawn from a Pareto distribution. Dashed black lines at ±5% delimit the region of negligible bias, and orange lines at ±20% the region of severe bias. Source: THEILUMINA team, preliminary results.



Research questions (WP2)

RQ5. Under which combinations of sample size, skewness and inequality do the asymptotic, bootstrap, semiparametric and jackknife variance estimators become unreliable?
RQ6. Can new jackknife-based variance estimators and confidence intervals achieve coverage close to the nominal level under strong skewness and inequality, both for the indices and for their decomposition?

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 3 · The jackknife is computationally prohibitive
text:
Problem 3 · The jackknife is computationally prohibitive
The jackknife recomputes the estimator n times, leaving out one observation each time, so its cost grows quadratically with the sample size (\mathcal{O}(n^2)). With n = 100{,}000 observations, the standard jackknife needs more than 16 minutes to compute the variance of a single Theil index, and a Monte Carlo study with n = 5{,}000 takes more than two days. Our closed-form expressions give exactly the same result with linear cost (\mathcal{O}(n)): 15 milliseconds and less than 40 seconds, respectively. For the bias-corrected estimators, the standard jackknife would take decades, which makes reduced expressions essential.



Computation times, in R, of the standard jackknife, the proposed closed-form jackknife and the asymptotic variance estimators of T_0 and T_1. Top: large samples (n up to 100,000). Bottom: complete Monte Carlo experiment (48,000 samples per sample size). Note the change of units: minutes and days for the standard jackknife, seconds for the proposed expressions. Source: THEILUMINA team, preliminary results.



Research questions (WP3)

RQ7. How large is the computational cost of the standard jackknife compared with alternative variance estimators for big data (surveys and administrative records with millions of observations)?
RQ8. Can exact, closed-form jackknife expressions be derived for the bias-corrected estimators, the decomposition components and complex survey designs, with no loss of accuracy?

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 4 · There is no open software for reliable Theil inference
text:
Problem 4 · There is no open software for reliable Theil inference
Existing software computes point estimates of Theil indices but does not offer bias diagnostics, bias corrections or reliable variance estimators and confidence intervals, and it does not scale to large samples.

Research question (WP4)

RQ9. Can the methods developed in WP1–WP3 be implemented in an open, documented and efficient R package (theil, with a C++ core) that makes reliable inference for Theil indices accessible to applied researchers?

title: Research problems and questions
section: Problem 5 · Do corrected estimates change empirical conclusions?
text:
Problem 5 · Do corrected estimates change empirical conclusions?
The bias is not a technicality. When the methods are applied to real data, the difference between standard and bias-corrected estimates varies with sample size, skewness and inequality, and can change rankings and conclusions. For example, in our application to real GDP per capita for 183 countries (1990–2023), the bias-corrected estimates are between 2% and 6% higher for T_0, and up to 12% higher for T_1, than the standard ones, with the largest differences in the most skewed regions (the Americas and Asia & Pacific).

Research questions (WP5)

RQ10. How unequal are household water consumption and expenditure between and within municipalities, and how much does the bias correction change this picture?
RQ11. Does tourism reduce or increase income inequality within and between destinations?
RQ12. How unequal are servitization, digital transformation and AI adoption across firms, sectors and countries?
RQ13. Is there global convergence in per capita consumption and income once bias-corrected estimators and reliable confidence intervals are used?


See Objectives, work packages and activities for how these questions are organised into work packages.
